sub: Named after its opening word, ar-Raḥmān, “the Most Merciful”
theme: Allah’s mercy, shown favour by favour: the Quran, creation, provision and the seas. Humans and jinn are asked again and again which favour they deny, then shown the Judgement, Hell, and two ranks of gardens.
story: Most reports place it in Makkah, very early; a few say Madinah. Before the command to preach openly, Makkans heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting its refrain in prayer at the Kaʿbah. ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd recited it aloud to the Quraysh there. They beat his face, and he kept reciting.

The Makkans did not know the name ar-Raḥmān and asked, “What is ar-Raḥmān?” Reportedly the surah came as the answer, or as a reply to their claim that a human was teaching the Prophet ﷺ. So it opens with that name and lists His favours.

It speaks to humans and jinn together throughout. Once the Prophet ﷺ recited it to his Companions and they stayed silent. He told them the jinn had answered better: at every refrain they said, “None of Your favours, our Lord, do we deny. All praise is Yours.”

sections.title: The Most Merciful taught the Quran, set the balance, spread earth’s provisions
sections.meaning: Ar-Raḥmān taught the Quran, created man and taught him to speak. The sun and moon keep exact courses; stars and trees bow to Him. He raised the sky and set the balance, so weigh fairly. He laid out the earth with fruit, palms and grain. Which favour will you deny?
points: The Most Merciful taught the Quran, created man, taught him speech
Sun and moon on exact courses; stars and trees bow
Sky raised, balance set: weigh fairly, never cut it short
Earth laid out for creatures: fruit, palms, grain, fragrant plants
First refrain: which of your Lord’s favours will you both deny?
sections.matters: It sets up the whole surah: every favour points back to ar-Raḥmān, and the first refrain asks humans and jinn to admit them. The Quran is named even before man’s creation, and the balance in the universe is tied to fairness in our own dealings.
sections.story: Reportedly revealed when the Makkans asked, “What is ar-Raḥmān?”, or in reply to their claim that a human was teaching the Prophet ﷺ. So it opens with that very name.
explained: The surah opens with one word, ar-Raḥmān, then His greatest gift: He taught the Quran and made it easy to learn. It comes before man’s creation, because man was made to follow its guidance. Then He gave man al-bayān, the power to express himself in speech and writing.

The sun and moon run bi-ḥusbān, on courses that never slip. Stars, or stemless plants, and trees bow by doing what they were made for. He raised the sky and set al-mīzān, justice, so never cheat on the scale. The earth holds fruit, sheathed palms, grain and fragrant plants. Which favour will you deny?
teaches: The Quran is the first favour named, even before our creation.
Speech is a gift: use it to learn the truth and pass it on.
The universe runs on balance, so our dealings must be fair.
Never cut short a weight, a measure or anyone’s right.
Meet every reminder of a favour with thanks, not denial.
sections.hook: Ayah 1 is a single word. ʿAllama opens 2 and 4, with khalaqa al-insān between. Al-mīzān appears three times in 7–9. The refrain appears for the first time at 13.

sections.title: Man from clay, jinn from fire; two easts, two seas, great ships
sections.meaning: Man was made from ringing clay and the jinn from pure flame. Allah is Lord of the two sunrises and two sunsets. He lets the sweet and salty seas meet with a barrier between them, brings pearls and coral out of them, and owns the ships that tower like mountains.
points: Man from ringing clay, jinn from smokeless flame
Lord of the two sunrises and the two sunsets
Two seas meet, but a barrier keeps them apart
Pearls and coral come out of them
His are the ships, tall as mountains at sea
sections.matters: Section 1 listed gifts to man; now the jinn stand beside him, and the refrain comes after almost every sign. These are signs anyone can see: the horizon, the sea, and the ships that carry people and their trade.
sections.story: No specific incident. It keeps listing Allah’s favours to humans and jinn, the two beings the refrain speaks to.
explained: Man, meaning Ādam, was made from ṣalṣāl: clay dried until it rings like baked pottery. The jinn were made from mārij, the pure tip of a flame. Allah is Lord of al-mashriqayn and al-maghribayn: where the sun rises and sets in summer and in winter, with all the benefits those seasons bring.

He let the two seas loose, sweet and salty, so they meet, yet a barzakh, a barrier set by His power, keeps each from spoiling the other. Pearls and marjān, coral or small pearls, come from them. And His are the ships raised high like mountains, carrying people and cargo. After each sign, the same question returns.
teaches: Humans and jinn were both created, and both owe thanks.
Changing sunrises and seasons bring benefits planned by Allah.
Allah keeps apart what would spoil each other if mixed.
Travel, trade and treasures from the sea are all His favours.
sections.hook: Nearly everything comes in twos: two creations (14–15), two easts and two wests (17), two seas (19), pearl and coral (22). The refrain closes 16, 18, 21, 23 and 25.

sections.title: Everyone on earth perishes but Allah; humans and jinn cannot escape judgement
sections.meaning: Everyone on earth will perish; only your Lord remains, full of majesty and honour. All in the heavens and earth ask Him, and every day He is at work. Soon He will turn to judging humans and jinn. Escape His realm if you can: you can’t. Flame and smoke would drive you back.
points: All on earth perish; your Lord’s Face remains
Everyone asks Him; every day He is at work
Soon We will attend to you, O two weighty beings
Escape the heavens and earth if you can: you can’t
Flame and smoke sent on you; no one can help
sections.matters: The second ruku turns from favours to endings. Everything passes, everyone depends on Allah, and the reckoning is coming with no way out. Even this warning counts as a favour, because it turns people away from sin.
sections.story: No specific incident for most of it. Reportedly “every day He is at work” (29) answered some Jews who claimed Allah decides nothing on the Sabbath.
explained: Kullu man ʿalayhā fān: every living thing on earth dies. Only wajhu rabbik remains, your Lord Himself, dhū al-jalāli wal-ikrām, Owner of Majesty and of the Honour He gives His friends. Everything in the heavens and earth asks Him for its needs, and every day He is fī shaʾn: giving life and death, raising and lowering, answering those who call.

Sanafrughu lakum, “We will attend to you,” is a warning of the reckoning; nothing ever keeps Allah busy. Ath-thaqalān, humans and jinn, are challenged: pass beyond the regions of the heavens and earth, if you can. You can’t, without a power you don’t have. Flame and smoke would be sent at you, and no one could defend you.
teaches: Everything you own and love will end; only Allah remains.
Take every need to Allah; He never tires of being asked.
Nothing can distract Allah from anyone.
There is no running from death or from judgement.
A warning is a mercy if it turns you back.
sections.hook: The second ruku opens with kullu man ʿalayhā fān (26). Dhū al-jalāli wal-ikrām (27) returns in the last ayah (78). Humans and jinn are named twice: ath-thaqalān (31), maʿshar al-jinni wal-ins (33).

sections.title: The sky splits red; criminals known by marks are dragged to Hell
sections.meaning: When the sky splits and turns red like oil, no one needs asking about his sin. Criminals are known by their marks and seized by forelocks and feet. They are shown the Hell they denied, and go back and forth between its fire and boiling water.
points: The sky splits and turns rose-red like oil
No human or jinn is asked about his sin
Criminals known by marks, seized by forelocks and feet
This is the Hell they denied; fire and boiling water
sections.matters: Section 3 warned that the reckoning is coming; this section shows it arriving. The criminals who called Hell a lie now see it before their eyes. Believing then is too late: belief counts only before the unseen is shown.
sections.story: No specific incident. It shows the end of those, human or jinn, who disobeyed Allah in this world.
explained: On the Day of Resurrection the sky splits open and becomes wardah kad-dihān: rose-red, melting and changing colour like oil. Then no human or jinn is asked whether he sinned. Allah already knows and the angels wrote it down. They are questioned at another stage, or asked only why, or simply recognised by their faces.

The criminals are known by dark faces and blue eyes, grabbed by forelocks and feet, and thrown into the Fire. They are told: hādhihi jahannam, this is the Hell you called a lie. They go back and forth between its flames and ḥamīm ān, water boiled to its very limit.
teaches: Nothing is hidden from Allah; every deed is already recorded.
Sins leave marks that will show on that Day.
What people deny today they will see tomorrow.
Believe now; belief after seeing it will not help.
sections.hook: Up to 42 the refrain falls on even ayat. Then 43–44 run back to back, and from 45 to 77 it falls on every odd ayah. Al-mujrimūn appears in 41 and 43.

sections.title: Two gardens for whoever fears standing before his Lord: fruit, springs, spouses
sections.meaning: Whoever feared standing before his Lord, and so left sin, gets two gardens: spreading branches, two flowing springs, every fruit in two kinds. They recline on couches lined with brocade, fruit within reach, with chaste spouses like rubies and coral. Is the reward for good anything but good?
points: Two gardens for whoever fears standing before his Lord
Spreading branches and two flowing springs
Every fruit in pairs; couches of brocade, fruit close
Spouses with lowered gaze, like rubies and coral
Is the reward for good anything but good?
sections.matters: After Hell comes the reward, and the third ruku, the surah’s longest, is given over to it. It names the quality that earns it, fearing the moment you stand before Allah, and ends with a rule: goodness is repaid with goodness.
sections.story: Reportedly ayah 46 was about Abū Bakr: either after he spoke one day of Paradise and Hell, or after he made himself vomit milk he learned was unlawful, and the Prophet ﷺ told him an ayah had come about him.
explained: Maqāma rabbih: standing before his Lord for the reckoning, or his Lord watching over him. Whoever fears it leaves sin, does what he is told, and receives two gardens. These are the higher pair, for those brought near to Allah, and the promise includes believing jinn.

The gardens have afnān, spreading branches heavy with fruit. Two springs flow freely, and every fruit comes in two kinds. The people recline on couches whose linings are thick silk brocade; if that is the lining, imagine the outside. The fruit hangs low enough to pick sitting or lying down.

Their spouses keep their gaze only on them, untouched by anyone before, pure as rubies and white as coral. Then the rule behind it all: hal jazāʾ al-iḥsāni illā al-iḥsān, is the reward for good anything but good?
teaches: Fearing to stand before Allah is what keeps a person from sin.
Paradise has ranks, so aim for the highest.
Nothing in this world compares to Paradise except in name.
Do good, and expect good back from Allah.
sections.hook: Jannatān (46) returns as al-jannatayn (54). Fīhimā (in both) opens 50 and 52; fīhinna opens 56. Every content ayah is even and every refrain odd, from 46 to 61.

sections.title: Two more gardens a rank below, then: blessed is your Lord’s name
sections.meaning: Below the first two are two more gardens: deep green, with gushing springs, fruit, palms and pomegranates. In them are good, beautiful spouses sheltered in pavilions, untouched before. The people recline on green cushions and fine carpets. The surah closes: blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour.
points: Two more gardens below them, dark green
Gushing springs; fruit, palms and pomegranates
Good, beautiful spouses sheltered in pavilions, untouched
Reclining on green cushions and fine carpets
Blessed is your Lord’s name, Owner of Majesty and Honour
sections.matters: It shows that Paradise has levels: these gardens are for the people of the right, a rank below those brought near. Comparing the two descriptions line by line shows the difference. The last ayah sums up the whole surah: every favour comes from His blessed name.
sections.story: No specific incident. Reportedly the Prophet ﷺ described two gardens of gold and two of silver; the gold are for those brought near, the silver for the people of the right.
explained: Min dūnihimā: below the first two, in rank. The first pair came first and had spreading branches, free-flowing springs and every fruit in pairs. These are mudhāmmatān, so green from watering they look dark, with naḍḍākhatān, gushing springs, and simply fruit, palms and pomegranates.

In them are khayrāt ḥisān, women good in character and beautiful in face, ḥūr sheltered in pavilions. The people recline on green rafraf, cushions or spreads, and ʿabqarī, fine rich carpets. Then the surah closes: tabāraka ismu rabbik, blessed is your Lord’s name, Owner of Majesty and Honour.
teaches: Paradise has levels, and even the lowest is beyond imagining.
Good character is named before beauty.
Strive for the higher rank; every level is a great favour.
Praise Allah as Owner of Majesty and Honour, as the Prophet ﷺ did after prayer.
sections.hook: The lines mirror section 5: afnān (48) becomes mudhāmmatān (64), tajriyān (50) becomes naḍḍākhatān (66), and lam yaṭmithhunna repeats exactly (56, 74). Ayah 78 echoes dhū al-jalāli wal-ikrām from 27.

groups.text: Ar-Raḥmān taught the Quran, created man, and taught him to express himself.
The sun and moon run on exact courses; the stars and trees bow to Him.
He raised the sky and set the balance, so do not cheat: weigh with fairness.
He laid out the earth with fruit, sheathed palms, grain and fragrant plants. Which of your Lord’s favours will you both deny?
Man was made from ringing clay, the jinn from pure flame. Which favour will you deny?
He is Lord of the two sunrises and the two sunsets. Which favour will you deny?
He lets the sweet and salty seas meet, with a barrier neither crosses. Which favour will you deny?
Pearls and coral come out of them. Which favour will you deny?
His are the ships raised high in the sea like mountains. Which favour will you deny?
Everyone on earth perishes; only your Lord remains, Owner of Majesty and Honour. Which favour will you deny?
All in the heavens and earth ask Him; every day He is at work. Which favour will you deny?
Soon We will attend to you, humans and jinn. Which favour will you deny?
Pass beyond the heavens and earth if you can; you cannot without power. Which favour will you deny?
Flame and smoke will be sent on you, and no one can help. Which favour will you deny?
The sky splits and turns rose-red like oil. Which favour will you deny?
That Day no human or jinn is asked about his sin. Which favour will you deny?
Criminals are known by their marks and seized by forelocks and feet. Which favour will you deny?
This is the Hell they denied; they go between it and boiling water. Which favour will you deny?
Whoever fears standing before his Lord gets two gardens. Which favour will you deny?
Both gardens have spreading branches and two flowing springs. Which favour will you deny?
In both is every fruit in two kinds. Which favour will you deny?
They recline on couches lined with brocade, the fruit hanging close. Which favour will you deny?
Spouses with lowered gaze, untouched before, like rubies and coral. Which favour will you deny?
Is the reward for good anything but good? Which favour will you deny?
Below those are two more gardens, dark green. Which favour will you deny?
In both are gushing springs, fruit, palms and pomegranates. Which favour will you deny?
In them are good, beautiful women, sheltered in pavilions. Which favour will you deny?
Untouched before by human or jinn, they recline on green cushions and fine carpets. Which favour will you deny?
Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour.

1.explain: Ar-Raḥmān: the Most Merciful, whose mercy and goodness reach everything. The whole surah that follows lists what that mercy has given.
1.why: Reportedly revealed when the Makkans, who did not accept this name, asked: “What is ar-Raḥmān?”

2.explain: ʿAllama al-Qurʾān: He taught the Quran, its words and meanings, and made it easy to learn. Either He taught the Prophet ﷺ, who passed it on, or no one is named so that it covers everyone.
2.why: Another report: a reply to Makkans who said a human was teaching him, meaning Musaylimah, whom they called “the Raḥmān of Yamāmah.” The answer: ar-Raḥmān taught the Quran.

3.explain: Khalaqa al-insān: He created man, complete and well formed; either Ādam or all people. The Quran is named first because man was created to follow its guidance.

4.explain: ʿAllamahu al-bayān: He taught him to express what is inside him, in speech and writing. It sets humans apart from animals, and through it the Quran is learned and passed on.

5.explain: Bi-ḥusbān: by exact calculation. The sun and moon run fixed courses that never slip or break down, so people can count days, months and years.

6.explain: An-najm: either the stars or low plants with no stem. Ash-shajar: trees with trunks. Both yasjudān, bow to Allah, by doing exactly what they were made for.

7.explain: He raised the sky high like a roof over the earth, and set al-mīzān: justice between people, including real scales and measures.

8.explain: So that you do not taṭghaw, go beyond the limit, in weighing and judging. Heaven and earth were made on justice, and people must keep to it.

9.explain: Aqīmū al-wazna bil-qisṭ: keep the weight fair. Wa lā tukhsirū: and don’t make it short. One command, one prohibition: never cheat in weights and measures.

10.explain: Waḍaʿahā lil-anām: He laid the earth low and steady for all creatures, humans and jinn among them, to live, build and farm on.

11.explain: Fākihah: fruit eaten for pleasure. Palms are singled out, dhāt al-akmām, with sheaths around their clusters, because dates are food both fresh and dried.

12.explain: Al-ḥabb: grain like wheat and barley, dhū al-ʿaṣf, with husk and straw that feed animals. Ar-rayḥān: either fragrant plants, or provision in general.

13.explain: The first of 31 refrains. Ālāʾ: favours. Rabbikumā, “your Lord” in the dual, speaks to humans and jinn. The right reply is to admit the favours and praise Allah, as the jinn did.

14.explain: Khalaqa al-insān returns from ayah 3, now with the material: ṣalṣāl, dry clay that rings when tapped, like fakhkhār, baked pottery. Here man means Ādam.

15.explain: Al-jānn: the father of the jinn. Mārij min nār: the pure tip of a flame with no smoke. A hadith adds that the angels were created from light.

16.explain: The second refrain comes straight after both creations are named: bringing humans and jinn into being is itself a favour.

17.explain: Rabb al-mashriqayn wa rabb al-maghribayn: Lord of the sunrise points of summer and winter, and of their sunsets. Those shifts bring many benefits to people.

18.explain: Refrain after the sunrises and sunsets. Everything the sun rises and sets on is under His care.

19.explain: Maraja al-baḥrayn: He let loose the two seas, sweet water and salty, so that they meet.

20.explain: Barzakh: a barrier, whether a strip of land or one set by His power alone. Lā yabghiyān: neither oversteps onto the other, so each keeps its own qualities.

21.explain: Refrain after the two seas: sweet water for drinking and crops, salty water for fish and ships. Both are favours.

22.explain: Al-luʾluʾ: pearls. Al-marjān: coral, or small pearls. They come from salty water, but both seas are named together, as Arabic allows.

23.explain: Refrain after the jewels: the adornment people take from the sea is also His gift.

24.explain: Al-jawār al-munshaʾāt: ships with sails raised, standing in the sea kal-aʿlām, like mountains. They are His: He made the sea carry them, and people and cargo with them.

25.explain: Refrain closing the first ruku: ships carry goods from land to land. Which of these favours will you deny?

26.explain: Kullu man ʿalayhā fān: everyone on earth will perish: humans, jinn and animals. Death makes everyone equal. When reciting, don’t stop here; carry on to 27, which says who remains.

27.explain: Wajhu rabbik: your Lord Himself remains, the Ever-Living. Dhū al-jalāli wal-ikrām: Owner of Majesty, and of the Honour He gives His friends. The Prophet ﷺ urged calling on Him by this name often.

28.explain: Refrain after the ending of all things: after death, all come before the One who remains, to be judged fairly.

29.explain: Everyone in the heavens and earth asks Him: for provision, forgiveness, mercy. Kulla yawmin huwa fī shaʾn: all the time He is acting, giving life and death, raising and lowering, answering callers.
29.why: Reportedly revealed about some Jews who said Allah decrees nothing on the Sabbath.

30.explain: Refrain: every need met, every hardship lifted and every prayer answered is part of His daily work, and a favour.

31.explain: Sanafrughu lakum: “We will attend to you,” a warning of the reckoning. It does not mean Allah is busy now. Ath-thaqalān: the two weighty beings, humans and jinn.

32.explain: Refrain after the warning: being told in advance that the reckoning is coming is a favour in itself.

33.explain: Yā maʿshar al-jinni wal-ins: pass beyond the regions of the heavens and earth, to flee death or judgement, if you can. You can’t without sulṭān, power you don’t have. It shows their weakness.

34.explain: Refrain after the challenge: that Day the angels surround creation on every side, so there is nowhere to run.

35.explain: Shuwāẓ: a flame of fire. Nuḥās: smoke, or molten brass. If they try to flee, it drives them back, and they cannot help each other: fa-lā tantaṣirān.

36.explain: Refrain closing the warning: frightening people away from sin is itself a favour, a whip driving them toward the best reward.

37.explain: The sky splits open, with gates for the angels to come down. Wardah: rose-red. Kad-dihān: like oil, melting and changing colour, or like red leather.

38.explain: The refrain cuts in before the scene is finished. Being warned of that Day now, while belief still counts, is a favour.

39.explain: No human or jinn is asked whether he sinned: Allah already knows. Either they are questioned at another stage, or asked only why, or the angels need not ask because the marks show.

40.explain: Refrain after 39: every deed is already known to Allah and written by the angels, so nothing will be lost.

41.explain: Bi-sīmāhum: by their marks, dark faces and blue eyes. They are seized bin-nawāṣī wal-aqdām, by forelocks and feet, perhaps forelock pressed to feet, and thrown into the Fire.

42.explain: Refrain after the seizing: this frightening scene is shown in advance, while there is still time to turn back.

43.explain: They are told: hādhihi jahannam, this is the Hell the criminals called a lie. Now it is before their eyes, said to shame them.

44.explain: Yaṭūfūna: they go back and forth between the Fire and ḥamīm ān, water boiled to its limit. When they beg for relief from the heat, this is what they get.

45.explain: Refrain closing the second ruku. Warning of Hell is a favour too: it urges all creation to leave shirk and sin.

46.explain: Maqāma rabbih: standing before his Lord for the reckoning, or his Lord watching over him. Whoever fears it leaves sin and gets jannatān, two gardens: one, some say, for leaving sin and one for obeying.
46.why: Reportedly about Abū Bakr: either after he spoke one day about Paradise and Hell, or after he made himself vomit milk he learned was unlawful, and the Prophet ﷺ said an ayah had come about him.

47.explain: Refrain after the promise of two gardens. It is addressed to jinn too, so believing jinn are promised these gardens as well.

48.explain: Dhawātā afnān: both full of branches, spreading and touching, heavy with ripe fruit. Or afnān means many kinds of delight.

49.explain: Refrain after the branches. Only this first pair of gardens is described with afnān; the second pair is not.

50.explain: Fīhimā ʿaynāni tajriyān: in both are two springs flowing freely, watering the trees. Reportedly one is Tasnīm and the other Salsabīl.

51.explain: Refrain after the springs. Free-flowing springs rank above the gushing springs of the second pair (66).

52.explain: Min kulli fākihatin zawjān: every fruit in two kinds, perhaps fresh and dried, or familiar and new. Every fruit of this world is there, even bitter ones, but sweet.

53.explain: Refrain after the fruit. Nothing in this world is like what is there, except in name.

54.explain: Reclining on furush, couches lined with istabraq, thick silk brocade. If the linings are this fine, imagine the outside. Janā al-jannatayn dān: fruit close enough to pick sitting or lying down.

55.explain: Refrain after the couches: they sit settled and at ease, like kings on thrones, with the fruit coming to them.

56.explain: Fīhinna qāṣirāt aṭ-ṭarf: wives whose gaze is only for their husbands. Lam yaṭmithhunna: untouched before them by any human or jinn, which also shows that believing jinn enter Paradise.

57.explain: The refrain interrupts the description, which continues in 58: each detail is counted as a favour of its own.

58.explain: Kaʾannahunna al-yāqūtu wal-marjān: as if they were rubies in purity and coral, or pearls, in whiteness.

59.explain: Refrain after their beauty: a spouse who loves you and sees no one else is one of Paradise’s favours.

60.explain: Hal jazāʾ al-iḥsāni illā al-iḥsān: is the reward for doing good anything but good? Whoever did well in worship and toward people is treated well. Reportedly the Prophet ﷺ said: the reward for tawḥīd is Paradise.

61.explain: Refrain closing the first pair of gardens. Rewards like these come from Allah’s generosity; good deeds alone could never earn them.

62.explain: Wa min dūnihimā jannatān: below those two, two more gardens, lower in rank. The first pair is for those brought near to Allah; this pair for the people of the right.

63.explain: Refrain after the second pair is announced: even the lower rank of Paradise is far beyond anything in this world.

64.explain: Mudhāmmatān: a whole ayah in one word, like ayah 1. So deep green from abundant water that the gardens look almost black.

65.explain: Refrain after the colour. The first pair was described by its branches (48); this pair by its deep green.

66.explain: Fīhimā ʿaynāni naḍḍākhatān: two springs gushing, never running dry. Compare 50: flowing springs are the higher quality.

67.explain: Refrain after the gushing springs. Reportedly they gush with goodness and blessing, or with musk and camphor, over the people of Paradise.

68.explain: Fākihatun wa nakhlun wa rummān: fruit, palms and pomegranates. Palms and pomegranates are fruit too, named for their special benefits. The first pair had “every fruit in two kinds” (52).

69.explain: Refrain after the fruit. Reportedly the palms of Paradise have trunks of green emerald and dates whiter than milk and sweeter than honey.

70.explain: Fīhinna khayrātun ḥisān: khayrāt, good in character, and ḥisān, beautiful in face. Reportedly the Prophet ﷺ explained it this way. Another view: all kinds of good things.

71.explain: Refrain after inner and outer beauty are named together, with character named first.

72.explain: Ḥūr: with strikingly dark and white eyes. Maqṣūrāt fī al-khiyām: sheltered in pavilions, each reportedly a single hollow pearl sixty miles wide.

73.explain: The refrain breaks in again mid-description; the description of the spouses runs on into 74.

74.explain: Lam yaṭmithhunna insun qablahum wa lā jānn: word for word the same as the end of ayah 56. Untouched before by any human or jinn.

75.explain: Refrain after the repeated line: this quality is shared by the spouses of both pairs of gardens.

76.explain: Muttakiʾīna ʿalā rafrafin khuḍr: reclining on green rafraf, cushions or spreads, and ʿabqariyyin ḥisān, finely woven rich carpets. Compare 54: couches lined with brocade.

77.explain: The 31st and last refrain. The jinn’s reply fits every time: none of Your favours, our Lord, do we deny.

78.explain: Tabāraka ismu rabbik: blessed and full of good is your Lord’s name, Owner of Majesty and Honour. After each prayer the Prophet ﷺ would say: “Blessed are You, Owner of Majesty and Honour.”
